CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the key metrics used to interpret usability test data, including error rates, task completion rates, and satisfaction scores.
Identify patterns and recurring issues within qualitative and quantitative usability test results.
Analyze error analysis data to determine the root causes of usability failures in an interface.
Evaluate usability findings to prioritize interface improvements based on severity and user impact.
Apply iterative redesign principles to refine and update prototype interfaces based on test findings.
Demonstrate the ability to document and communicate redesign decisions supported by usability evidence.

Topics.Title: Foundations of Usability Test Data
Topics.Summary: Introduces the types of data collected during usability testing and explains the distinction between quantitative and qualitative findings. Establishes a shared vocabulary for interpreting test results.

Elements.Title: Quantitative vs. Qualitative Data
Elements.BodyText: Usability tests produce two broad categories of data: quantitative measures that are numerical and statistically comparable, and qualitative observations that capture the richness of user behavior and experience.
Elements.Notes: Quantitative data answers 'how much' or 'how often,' while qualitative data answers 'why' and 'how.' Both are necessary for a complete picture of usability issues.

Items.Text: Quantitative data includes metrics such as task completion rates, time on task, and error counts.
Qualitative data includes think-aloud commentary, observed confusion, and post-task interview responses.
Combining both data types produces more actionable insights than relying on either alone.
Quantitative data enables comparison across iterations; qualitative data explains the reasons behind the numbers.

Elements.Title: Task Completion Rates
Elements.BodyText: Task completion rate measures the percentage of participants who successfully finish a defined task without assistance, making it one of the most direct indicators of interface effectiveness.
Elements.Notes: A task should be considered failed if the user gives up, requests help, or arrives at an incorrect outcome. Even partial completions can be tracked separately as a nuanced metric.

Items.Text: Task completion rates are calculated by dividing the number of successful completions by the total number of attempts.
Low completion rates on a specific task signal a critical usability problem requiring immediate attention.
Completion rates should always be analyzed in context with the task's complexity and user familiarity.
Tracking completion rates across iterations reveals whether redesign efforts have improved usability.

Elements.Title: Error Rate Analysis
Elements.BodyText: Error rate measures how frequently users make mistakes while attempting to complete tasks, providing insight into which interface elements cause confusion or misdirection.
Elements.Notes: Errors can be slips (execution mistakes) or mistakes (planning errors). Distinguishing between them helps target whether the interface needs clearer affordances or better information architecture.

Items.Text: Error rate is calculated as the number of errors divided by the total number of opportunities for error.
Recurring errors on the same element indicate a systematic design flaw rather than a one-time user slip.
Both the frequency and the severity of errors must be considered when prioritizing fixes.
Cataloging error types helps distinguish between navigation errors, input errors, and comprehension errors.

Elements.Title: Time on Task
Elements.BodyText: Time on task measures how long a user takes to complete a given activity, serving as a proxy for efficiency and learnability of the interface.
Elements.Notes: Unusually long task times may indicate that users are lost, confused, or exploring unintended paths. However, very short times can sometimes indicate that users skipped steps or misunderstood the task.

Items.Text: Time on task is measured from when the user begins a task to when they declare completion or abandon it.
Benchmarking time on task against expert performance reveals how much the design slows novice users.
Significant drops in time on task between test iterations indicate successful usability improvements.
Outlier times — both very high and very low — should be investigated for underlying causes.

Elements.Title: Satisfaction Scores
Elements.BodyText: Satisfaction scores capture the subjective user perception of the interface through standardized questionnaires, providing a self-reported measure of usability and emotional response.
Elements.Notes: Common instruments include the System Usability Scale (SUS), the Net Promoter Score (NPS), and the Single Ease Question (SEQ). SUS scores above 68 are generally considered above average.

Items.Text: Satisfaction scores complement behavioral data by revealing how users feel about the interface, not just how they perform.
Standardized scales like the SUS allow for benchmarking against industry norms and competing products.
Post-task satisfaction scores capture immediate reactions, while post-session scores reflect the overall experience.
A gap between high task performance and low satisfaction may indicate hidden frustration or lack of confidence.

Topics.Title: Collecting and Organizing Test Data
Topics.Summary: Covers practical methods for capturing usability data during sessions and structuring it for efficient analysis. Emphasizes the importance of consistent recording practices across participants.

Elements.Title: Data Collection Methods
Elements.BodyText: Reliable analysis depends on consistent and thorough data collection during test sessions, using a combination of automated tools, observer notes, and recording technologies.
Elements.Notes: Screen recording software, eye-tracking tools, and note-taking templates all serve different purposes. Teams should decide in advance which data points are most critical for their research questions.

Items.Text: Screen and audio recordings capture interactions and think-aloud commentary for later review.
Observers should use structured note-taking templates to ensure consistent data capture across sessions.
Automated analytics tools can log clicks, errors, and time stamps without observer bias.
Multiple observers increase data reliability but require a shared coding scheme to ensure consistency.

Elements.Title: Affinity Diagramming
Elements.BodyText: Affinity diagramming is a collaborative method for grouping qualitative observations into thematic clusters, making it easier to identify patterns across multiple participants.
Elements.Notes: Each observation is written on a separate note, and the team physically or digitally groups related notes. This process surfaces unexpected themes that structured analysis might miss.

Items.Text: Each discrete observation or quote from a test session is recorded as a single unit on a note or card.
Notes are grouped by similarity to reveal recurring themes and shared pain points.
Affinity diagrams are most effective when built collaboratively by the full design team.
The resulting clusters directly inform which usability issues are widespread versus isolated.

Elements.Title: Usability Issue Logs
Elements.BodyText: A usability issue log is a structured document that records each identified problem along with contextual information needed to understand and address it.
Elements.Notes: Issue logs typically include columns for the issue description, the affected task or screen, frequency of occurrence, severity rating, and recommended action. Keeping this document updated across iterations supports longitudinal tracking.

Items.Text: Each entry in the log should describe the problem, not the solution, to keep analysis objective.
Recording the frequency and severity of each issue allows for data-driven prioritization.
Issue logs serve as an audit trail that connects design decisions to specific user observations.
Sharing the issue log with stakeholders provides transparent evidence for redesign requests.

Elements.Title: Synthesizing Across Participants
Elements.BodyText: Analysis must look across all participants to distinguish widespread usability failures from individual edge cases, ensuring that redesign efforts address the broadest possible impact.
Elements.Notes: With small usability samples (typically 5–8 participants), patterns seen in three or more users are generally considered significant. Statistical significance is less relevant than practical significance in most formative usability studies.

Items.Text: Issues observed by multiple participants carry more redesign priority than those seen only once.
Cross-participant synthesis helps separate systematic design flaws from individual user differences.
Frequency tables or heat maps can visualize where errors and struggles concentrate across the interface.
Synthesis should be completed promptly after sessions while observer memories are still fresh.

Topics.Title: Interpreting Error Analysis
Topics.Summary: Provides frameworks for classifying and diagnosing user errors to identify their root causes within the interface design. Helps students move from symptom identification to actionable diagnosis.

Elements.Title: Classifying Error Types
Elements.BodyText: Not all errors are equal — distinguishing between different error types allows designers to target the correct layer of the interface when implementing fixes.
Elements.Notes: Norman's slip-versus-mistake distinction is a useful starting framework: slips occur when users know the right action but execute incorrectly, while mistakes reflect flawed mental models or misunderstood system logic.

Items.Text: Slips are execution errors caused by automatic behavior or motor misfires and often indicate poor affordance design.
Mistakes are knowledge-based errors stemming from incorrect understanding of system behavior or task logic.
Navigation errors indicate problems with information architecture or wayfinding cues.
Input errors suggest inadequate field labels, format guidance, or validation feedback.

Elements.Title: Root Cause Analysis
Elements.BodyText: Root cause analysis moves beyond describing what went wrong to diagnosing why, connecting interface design choices to specific user failures.
Elements.Notes: The '5 Whys' technique — asking 'why' repeatedly until the underlying cause is uncovered — is a simple but effective tool for driving root cause analysis in a design context.

Items.Text: Each documented error should be traced back to a specific design decision or missing design element.
Asking 'why did this happen?' repeatedly helps avoid treating symptoms rather than underlying causes.
Root causes often fall into categories such as unclear labeling, hidden affordances, or missing feedback.
Addressing root causes prevents the same class of error from recurring in different parts of the interface.

Elements.Title: Mapping Errors to Interface Elements
Elements.BodyText: Linking specific errors to the exact interface elements that caused them creates a direct connection between the analysis and the redesign work that follows.
Elements.Notes: Annotated screenshots or wireframes can serve as visual maps showing where errors cluster. This artifact is especially useful for communicating findings to developers or stakeholders.

Items.Text: Error mapping pinpoints which screens, components, or interaction flows are most problematic.
Visual error maps make patterns immediately apparent to team members who did not observe the sessions.
High error density around a single element suggests a fundamental design flaw rather than a minor adjustment.
Error maps should be updated after each redesign iteration to track improvement or regression.

Elements.Title: Distinguishing Critical from Minor Errors
Elements.BodyText: Errors vary in their impact on the user experience, and correctly distinguishing critical failures from minor inconveniences is essential for efficient resource allocation in redesign.
Elements.Notes: Critical errors are those that prevent task completion or cause data loss. Minor errors slow users down but do not block progress. A severity scale (e.g., 1–4) applied consistently across all issues supports fair comparison.

Items.Text: Critical errors prevent task completion and must be addressed before the next usability test iteration.
Minor errors reduce efficiency or satisfaction but do not block users from achieving their goals.
Severity ratings should consider both the frequency of the error and its consequence when it occurs.
Applying a consistent severity scale across all issues enables objective, data-driven prioritization.

Topics.Title: Prioritizing Usability Improvements
Topics.Summary: Introduces frameworks for ranking identified usability issues so that the most impactful problems are addressed first. Helps students make principled trade-offs when resources and time are limited.

Elements.Title: Severity Rating Frameworks
Elements.BodyText: Severity rating frameworks provide a systematic way to score usability issues so that teams can rank them objectively rather than relying on intuition or internal politics.
Elements.Notes: Nielsen's severity rating scale combines frequency, impact, and persistence into a score from 0 (not a usability problem) to 4 (usability catastrophe). Using such a scale consistently enables fair comparison across different types of issues.

Items.Text: Severity scores typically combine the frequency of an issue with the magnitude of its impact on users.
Applying a standard severity scale ensures that all team members evaluate issues using the same criteria.
High-severity issues should be addressed in the immediate redesign iteration regardless of implementation difficulty.
Severity ratings should be revisited after each iteration to confirm whether interventions were effective.

Elements.Title: Impact vs. Effort Mapping
Elements.BodyText: Impact versus effort mapping plots usability issues on a two-axis grid to identify quick wins — high-impact fixes that require minimal effort — and to deprioritize low-impact, high-effort changes.
Elements.Notes: This approach is particularly useful when working with limited development resources. It is also helpful for building stakeholder buy-in by demonstrating early, visible improvements through quick wins.

Items.Text: High-impact, low-effort issues represent quick wins that should be addressed immediately.
High-impact, high-effort issues require planning and should be scheduled for future iterations.
Low-impact, low-effort issues can be addressed opportunistically during routine development work.
Low-impact, high-effort issues should generally be deprioritized or removed from scope.

Elements.Title: Aligning Priorities with Design Goals
Elements.BodyText: Prioritization must be anchored to the core usability goals and user needs established at the start of the project, ensuring that fixes reinforce rather than undermine the intended user experience.
Elements.Notes: Design teams sometimes over-index on aesthetic or technically interesting fixes rather than those most relevant to user goals. Returning to original personas, user journeys, and success metrics helps maintain alignment.

Items.Text: Each prioritized issue should be evaluated against the product's defined usability goals and user requirements.
Fixes that address the primary user tasks should take precedence over those affecting secondary features.
Stakeholder priorities and user priorities may diverge and must be reconciled transparently.
Documenting the rationale for prioritization decisions ensures accountability and supports future retrospectives.

Elements.Title: Communicating Priorities to Stakeholders
Elements.BodyText: Translating usability findings into a clear, evidence-based priority list is essential for gaining stakeholder support and aligning cross-functional teams on redesign decisions.
Elements.Notes: Non-technical stakeholders respond well to visual summaries — such as annotated screenshots, short video clips of user struggles, and simple charts — rather than dense data tables. Framing issues in terms of business impact (e.g., drop-off rates, support costs) can strengthen the case.

Items.Text: Findings should be presented visually and concisely, avoiding jargon that may alienate non-design stakeholders.
Connecting usability issues to business outcomes such as conversion rates or customer satisfaction scores increases stakeholder urgency.
A prioritized issue list with severity ratings provides a shared reference point for cross-team planning.
Short video clips of users struggling are often the most persuasive evidence for non-technical audiences.

Topics.Title: Principles of Iterative Redesign
Topics.Summary: Establishes the conceptual foundation for iterative design as a cyclical process of testing, learning, and improving. Distinguishes iterative refinement from wholesale redesign.

Elements.Title: The Iterative Design Cycle
Elements.BodyText: Iterative design is a repeating process in which each round of testing produces findings that inform targeted improvements, which are then tested again in the next cycle.
Elements.Notes: The core cycle is often described as: prototype → test → analyze → redesign → repeat. The number of iterations depends on available resources and the severity of remaining issues. Most professional usability programs conduct at least two to three iterations.

Items.Text: Each iteration should begin with a clear set of hypotheses about what changes will address the identified issues.
Iterations narrow the scope of changes over time as major issues are resolved and refinements become more incremental.
Testing after each iteration confirms whether changes improved usability or introduced new problems.
The iterative cycle continues until usability metrics meet predefined success criteria or resources are exhausted.

Elements.Title: Targeted vs. Wholesale Redesign
Elements.BodyText: Effective iterative redesign involves making targeted, evidence-based changes to specific problem areas rather than reimagining the entire interface after each round of testing.
Elements.Notes: Wholesale redesigns between test iterations make it difficult to isolate which changes caused observed improvements or regressions. Targeted changes support clearer cause-and-effect analysis.

Items.Text: Targeted changes allow teams to attribute improvements or regressions directly to specific design decisions.
Redesigning only what the evidence demands conserves resources and minimizes the risk of introducing new problems.
Wholesale redesigns are appropriate only when foundational structural problems make targeted fixes insufficient.
Each change should be traceable to a specific usability finding documented in the issue log.

Elements.Title: Maintaining Design Rationale
Elements.BodyText: Design rationale documentation records the reasoning behind each redesign decision, creating an institutional memory that prevents teams from inadvertently reverting to previously tested and rejected solutions.
Elements.Notes: Design rationale can be maintained in a decision log, annotated wireframe history, or version-controlled design file. This documentation is especially valuable when team members change between iterations.

Items.Text: Each design change should be documented with the usability evidence that motivated it.
Design rationale prevents teams from repeatedly debating decisions that have already been resolved through testing.
Historical documentation supports onboarding new team members and briefing stakeholders on design evolution.
Version-controlled design files paired with a decision log create a complete audit trail of the redesign process.

Elements.Title: Setting Success Criteria for Each Iteration
Elements.BodyText: Before beginning a redesign iteration, teams should establish measurable success criteria that define what 'better' looks like for the issues being addressed.
Elements.Notes: Success criteria might specify a target task completion rate, a maximum acceptable error rate, or a minimum SUS score. Without pre-defined criteria, it is difficult to determine when an issue has been sufficiently resolved.

Items.Text: Success criteria should be specific, measurable, and directly tied to the usability issues being addressed.
Pre-defined criteria prevent subjective debates about whether an iteration was successful.
Criteria should be set before testing begins to avoid post-hoc rationalization of results.
Unmet criteria signal that further iteration is needed before the design is ready for development or release.

Topics.Title: Implementing Redesign Changes in Prototypes
Topics.Summary: Guides students through the practical process of translating usability findings into concrete prototype revisions. Covers fidelity decisions, annotation practices, and version management.

Elements.Title: Choosing the Right Prototype Fidelity
Elements.BodyText: The fidelity of a prototype — from low-fidelity paper sketches to high-fidelity interactive mockups — should match the questions being tested in the next iteration rather than defaulting to the highest possible fidelity.
Elements.Notes: Early iterations with major structural problems benefit from low-fidelity prototypes because they are faster to revise. Later iterations focused on visual hierarchy, microcopy, or interaction timing benefit from higher fidelity.

Items.Text: Low-fidelity prototypes are appropriate for testing navigation structure, task flows, and information architecture changes.
High-fidelity prototypes are necessary when testing visual design decisions, animations, or subtle interaction patterns.
Choosing appropriate fidelity reduces waste by avoiding over-investment in details that may change again.
Fidelity decisions should be made based on the specific usability questions the next test iteration will answer.

Elements.Title: Translating Findings into Design Changes
Elements.BodyText: Each prioritized usability finding must be converted into a specific, actionable design change that addresses its root cause — not merely its surface symptom.
Elements.Notes: For each issue, designers should generate multiple possible solutions before selecting the most appropriate one. Ideation even at this stage prevents premature commitment to the first obvious fix.

Items.Text: Each design change should map directly to a specific issue entry in the usability issue log.
Multiple solution options should be generated and compared before committing to a change.
Changes should address root causes identified during error analysis, not just the visible symptom.
Proposed changes should be reviewed against established design heuristics before implementation.

Elements.Title: Annotating Redesigned Prototypes
Elements.BodyText: Annotations on redesigned prototypes explain the reasoning behind each change, making it easier for team members, developers, and stakeholders to understand the intent and context of updates.
Elements.Notes: Annotations are especially important in handoff scenarios where developers must implement designs without direct access to the design team. They also serve as documentation for future audit trails.

Items.Text: Each significant design change should be annotated with the usability finding that motivated it.
Annotations communicate design intent to developers and prevent misinterpretation during implementation.
Annotated prototypes can be shared with stakeholders as evidence that redesign decisions are evidence-based.
Annotations should be kept concise — one to two sentences — focusing on the 'why' rather than the 'what.'

Elements.Title: Version Management for Iterative Prototypes
Elements.BodyText: Managing prototype versions systematically ensures that previous iterations are preserved for comparison, preventing accidental loss of design history and enabling regression analysis.
Elements.Notes: Tools like Figma, InVision, or version-controlled file naming conventions (e.g., 'prototype_v2_post-test1') support effective version management. Teams should establish a naming and storage convention before the first iteration begins.

Items.Text: Each iteration of the prototype should be saved as a distinct version with a clear, consistent naming convention.
Preserved previous versions allow teams to compare before-and-after states when evaluating the impact of changes.
Version management prevents accidental overwriting of tested prototypes that may be needed for future reference.
A version changelog summarizing what changed between iterations supports team communication and stakeholder updates.

Elements.Title: Validating Changes Before the Next Test
Elements.BodyText: Before conducting the next formal usability test, teams should conduct informal internal reviews or expert walkthroughs of the redesigned prototype to catch obvious errors or unintended regressions.
Elements.Notes: Heuristic evaluations and cognitive walkthroughs are efficient pre-test validation methods. They do not replace user testing but can catch easily preventable problems before scarce testing resources are consumed.

Items.Text: Internal expert reviews can identify obvious usability problems introduced during the redesign process.
Cognitive walkthroughs simulate user thought processes step-by-step to verify that task flows remain coherent.
Pre-test validation reduces wasted testing sessions by catching critical errors before participants are involved.
Any issues found during validation should be corrected and logged before the next formal test session begins.

Topics.Title: Documenting and Communicating Redesign Outcomes
Topics.Summary: Covers how to produce clear documentation of the redesign process and communicate outcomes to team members, stakeholders, and future designers. Emphasizes evidence-based reporting as a professional practice.

Elements.Title: Usability Testing Reports
Elements.BodyText: A usability testing report synthesizes findings from a test session into a structured document that can be shared with the broader team and stakeholders to drive aligned decision-making.
Elements.Notes: Effective reports balance detail with accessibility — they should be thorough enough for designers to act on but clear enough for non-specialist stakeholders to understand. Executive summaries, visual evidence, and a prioritized issue list are key components.

Items.Text: A well-structured report includes an executive summary, methodology, key findings, and a prioritized recommendation list.
Visual evidence such as annotated screenshots and direct user quotes makes findings concrete and persuasive.
Reports should be written at a level of detail appropriate for their intended audience.
Distributing the report promptly after sessions ensures findings are acted upon while momentum is high.

Elements.Title: Before-and-After Comparison Documentation
Elements.BodyText: Side-by-side comparisons of prototype versions before and after redesign changes provide clear visual evidence of progress and help stakeholders appreciate the value of the iterative process.
Elements.Notes: Before-and-after comparisons are particularly effective in portfolio presentations, stakeholder reviews, and project retrospectives. Pairing visual comparisons with metric changes (e.g., task completion rate increased from 60% to 90%) creates a compelling narrative.

Items.Text: Before-and-after comparisons visually demonstrate the direct impact of usability-driven design decisions.
Pairing visual comparisons with quantitative metric changes strengthens the evidence for redesign effectiveness.
These documents are valuable artifacts for design portfolios demonstrating iterative, evidence-based practice.
Comparisons should highlight not just aesthetic changes but functional and interaction-level improvements.

Elements.Title: Tracking Metrics Across Iterations
Elements.BodyText: Tracking the same usability metrics — task completion rates, error rates, satisfaction scores — across multiple iterations creates a longitudinal view of how the design is improving over time.
Elements.Notes: A simple tracking table or dashboard that records metrics for each iteration makes trends immediately visible. Metrics that plateau despite continued changes may signal that a fundamentally different design approach is needed.

Items.Text: Consistent use of the same metrics and tasks across iterations enables valid before-and-after comparisons.
A longitudinal metrics table makes overall design progress transparent to the team and stakeholders.
Plateauing metrics may indicate that targeted fixes have been exhausted and a deeper redesign is needed.
Metric trends should be reviewed at the end of each iteration as part of the planning process for the next.

Elements.Title: Presenting Findings to Non-Technical Audiences
Elements.BodyText: Communicating usability findings effectively to non-technical stakeholders requires translating data-heavy analysis into clear narratives, visual evidence, and business-relevant framing.
Elements.Notes: Storytelling techniques — such as walking stakeholders through a user's struggle with a specific task — are often more persuasive than charts alone. The goal is to create empathy for the user experience, not just report statistics.

Items.Text: Lead with user impact — what users could not do — before presenting the data behind the findings.
Use plain language and avoid UX jargon when presenting to business or engineering stakeholders.
Video clips of user sessions are among the most powerful tools for creating stakeholder empathy.
Frame recommended changes in terms of expected improvements to business-relevant outcomes where possible.

Elements.Title: Lessons Learned and Process Reflection
Elements.BodyText: Reflecting on the testing and redesign process itself — not just the design outcomes — helps teams continuously improve their usability practice across projects.
Elements.Notes: End-of-iteration retrospectives that examine what worked, what did not, and what would be done differently build organizational learning. This practice is especially important in educational settings where students are developing their professional methods.

Items.Text: Retrospective reflection should examine both the quality of the design decisions and the effectiveness of the testing process.
Identifying what worked well in the testing process helps teams replicate successful practices in future projects.
Recognizing methodological weaknesses — such as biased task wording or unrepresentative participants — improves future test planning.
Lessons learned documentation creates institutional knowledge that benefits future projects and new team members.
